{{Short description|Function in q-analog theory}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''q''-gamma function}}
In [[q-analog]] theory, the '''<math>q</math>-gamma function''', or '''basic gamma function''', is a generalization of the ordinary [[gamma function]] closely related to the [[double gamma function]]. It was introduced by {{harvtxt|Jackson|1905}}. It is given by
<math display="block">\Gamma_q(x) = (1-q)^{1-x}\prod_{n=0}^\infty \frac{1-q^{n+1}}{1-q^{n+x}}=(1-q)^{1-x}\,\frac{(q;q)_\infty}{(q^x;q)_\infty}</math>
when <math>|q|<1</math>, and
<math display="block"> \Gamma_q(x)=\frac{(q^{-1};q^{-1})_\infty}{(q^{-x};q^{-1})_\infty}(q-1)^{1-x}q^{\binom{x}{2}} </math>
if <math>|q|>1</math>. Here <math>(\cdot;\cdot)_\infty</math> is the infinite [[q-Pochhammer symbol|<math>q</math>-Pochhammer symbol]]. The <math>q</math>-gamma function satisfies the functional equation
<math display="block">\Gamma_q(x+1) = \frac{1-q^{x}}{1-q}\Gamma_q(x)=[x]_q\Gamma_q(x)</math>
In addition, the <math>q</math>-gamma function satisfies the q-analog of the [[Bohr–Mollerup theorem]], which was found by [[Richard Askey]] ({{harvtxt|Askey|1978}}).

For non-negative integers <math>n</math>,
<math display="block">\Gamma_q(n)=[n-1]_q!</math>
where <math>[\cdot]_q</math> is the [[q-factorial|<math>q</math>-factorial]] function. Thus the <math>q</math>-gamma function can be considered as an extension of the <math>q</math>-factorial function to the real numbers.

The relation to the ordinary gamma function is made explicit in the limit
<math display="block">\lim_{q \to 1\pm} \Gamma_q(x) = \Gamma(x).</math>
There is a simple proof of this limit by Gosper. See the appendix of ({{harvs|txt|authorlink=George Andrews (mathematician)| last=Andrews| year=1986}}).

== Transformation properties ==
The <math>q</math>-gamma function satisfies the q-analog of the Gauss multiplication formula ({{harvtxt|Gasper|Rahman|2004}}):
<math display="block">\Gamma_q(nx)\Gamma_r(1/n)\Gamma_r(2/n)\cdots\Gamma_r((n-1)/n)=\left(\frac{1-q^n}{1-q}\right)^{nx-1}\Gamma_r(x)\Gamma_r(x+1/n)\cdots\Gamma_r(x+(n-1)/n), \ r=q^n.</math>

=== Integral representation ===
The <math>q</math>-gamma function has the following integral representation ({{harvs|txt|authorlink=Mourad E. H. Ismail| last=Ismail| year=1981}}):
<math display="block">\frac{1}{\Gamma_q(z)}=\frac{\sin(\pi z)}{\pi}\int_0^\infty\frac{t^{-z}\mathrm{d}t}{(-t(1-q);q)_{\infty}}.</math>

=== Stirling formula ===
Moak obtained the following q-analogue of the Stirling formula (see {{harvtxt|Moak|1984}}):
<math display="block">\log\Gamma_q(x)\sim(x-1/2)\log[x]_q+\frac{\mathrm{Li}_2(1-q^x)}{\log q}+C_{\hat{q}}+\frac{1}{2}H(q-1)\log q+\sum_{k=1}^\infty
\frac{B_{2k}}{(2k)!}\left(\frac{\log \hat{q}}{\hat{q}^x-1}\right)^{2k-1}\hat{q}^x p_{2k-3}(\hat{q}^x), \ x\to\infty,</math>
<math display="block">\hat{q}=
  \left\{\begin{aligned}
  q \quad \mathrm{if} \ &0<q\leq1 \\
  1/q \quad \mathrm{if} \ &q\geq1
\end{aligned}\right\},</math>
<math display="block">C_q = \frac{1}{2} \log(2\pi)+\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{q-1}{\log q}\right)-\frac{1}{24}\log q+\log\sum_{m=-\infty}^\infty \left(r^{m(6m+1)} - r^{(3m+1)(2m+1)}\right),</math>
where <math>r=\exp(4\pi^2/\log q)</math>, <math>H</math> denotes the [[Heaviside step function]], <math>B_k</math> stands for the [[Bernoulli number]], <math>\mathrm{Li}_2(z)</math> is the [[dilogarithm]], and <math>p_k</math> is a polynomial of degree <math>k</math> satisfying
<math display="block"> p_k(z)=z(1-z)p'_{k-1}(z)+(kz+1)p_{k-1}(z), p_0=p_{-1}=1, k=1,2,\cdots.</math>

== Raabe-type formulas ==

Due to I. Mező, the q-analogue of the [[Gamma function#Raabe.27s formula|Raabe formula]] exists, at least if we use the <math>q</math>-gamma function when <math>|q|>1</math>. With this restriction,
<math display="block"> \int_0^1\log\Gamma_q(x)dx=\frac{\zeta(2)}{\log q}+\log\sqrt{\frac{q-1}{\sqrt[6]{q}}}+\log(q^{-1};q^{-1})_\infty \quad(q>1). </math>
El Bachraoui considered the case <math>0<q<1</math> and proved that
<math display="block"> \int_0^1\log\Gamma_q(x)dx=\frac{1}{2}\log (1-q) - \frac{\zeta(2)}{\log q}+\log(q;q)_\infty \quad(0<q<1). </math>

== Special values ==

The following special values are known.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Mező |first=István |year=2011 |title=Several special values of Jacobi theta functions |eprint=1106.1042 |mode=cs2 |class=math.NT }}</ref>
<math display="block">\Gamma_{e^{-\pi}}\left(\frac12\right)=\frac{e^{-7 \pi /16} \sqrt{e^\pi-1}\sqrt[4]{1+\sqrt2}}{2^{15/16}\pi^{3/4}} \, \Gamma \left(\frac{1}{4}\right),</math>
<math display="block">\Gamma_{e^{-2\pi}}\left(\frac12\right)=\frac{e^{-7 \pi /8} \sqrt{e^{2 \pi}-1}}{2^{9/8} \pi^{3/4}} \, \Gamma \left(\frac{1}{4}\right),</math>
<math display="block">\Gamma_{e^{-4\pi}}\left(\frac12\right)=\frac{e^{-7 \pi /4} \sqrt{e^{4 \pi}-1}}{2^{7/4} \pi^{3/4}} \, \Gamma \left(\frac{1}{4}\right),</math>
<math display="block">\Gamma_{e^{-8\pi}}\left(\frac12\right)=\frac{e^{-7 \pi /2} \sqrt{e^{8 \pi}-1}}{2^{9/4} \pi^{3/4} \sqrt{1+\sqrt2}} \, \Gamma \left(\frac{1}{4}\right).</math>
These are the analogues of the classical formula <math>\Gamma\left(\frac12\right)=\sqrt\pi</math>.

Moreover, the following analogues of the familiar identity <math>\Gamma\left(\frac14\right)\Gamma\left(\frac34\right)=\sqrt2\pi</math> hold true:
<math display="block">\Gamma_{e^{-2\pi}}\left(\frac14\right)\Gamma_{e^{-2\pi}}\left(\frac34\right)=\frac{e^{-29 \pi /16} \left(e^{2 \pi }-1\right)\sqrt[4]{1+\sqrt2}}{2^{33/16} \pi^{3/2}} \, \Gamma \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2,</math>
<math display="block">\Gamma_{e^{-4\pi}}\left(\frac14\right)\Gamma_{e^{-4\pi}}\left(\frac34\right)=\frac{e^{-29 \pi /8} \left(e^{4 \pi }-1\right)}{2^{23/8} \pi ^{3/2}} \, \Gamma \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2,</math>
<math display="block">\Gamma_{e^{-8\pi}}\left(\frac14\right)\Gamma_{e^{-8\pi}}\left(\frac34\right)=\frac{e^{-29 \pi /4} \left(e^{8 \pi }-1\right)}{16 \pi ^{3/2} \sqrt{1+\sqrt2}} \, \Gamma \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2.</math>

== Matrix version ==
Let <math>A</math> be a complex [[square matrix]] and [[positive-definite matrix]]. Then a <math>q</math>-gamma matrix function can be defined by <math>q</math>-integral:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Salem |first1=Ahmed |date=June 2012 |title=On a ''q''-gamma and a ''q''-beta matrix functions |journal=Linear and Multilinear Algebra |volume=60 |issue=6 |pages=683–696 |doi=10.1080/03081087.2011.627562 | s2cid=123011613 }}</ref>
<math display="block">\Gamma_q(A):=\int_0^{\frac{1}{1-q}}t^{A-I}E_q(-qt)\mathrm{d}_q t </math>
where <math>E_q</math> is the [[q-exponential]] function.

== Other ''q''-gamma functions ==
For other <math>q</math>-gamma functions, see Yamasaki 2006.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yamasaki |first1=Yoshinori |title=On ''q''-Analogues of the Barnes Multiple Zeta Functions |journal=Tokyo Journal of Mathematics |date=December 2006 |volume=29 |issue=2 |pages=413–427 |arxiv=math/0412067 |doi=10.3836/tjm/1170348176 |mr=2284981 |zbl=1192.11060|s2cid=14082358 }}</ref>

== Numerical computation ==
An iterative algorithm to compute the q-gamma function was proposed by Gabutti and Allasia.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gabutti |first1=Bruno |last2=Allasia |first2=Giampietro |title=Evaluation of q-gamma function and q-analogues by iterative algorithms |journal=Numerical Algorithms |date=17 September 2008 |volume=49 |issue=1–4 |pages=159–168 |doi=10.1007/s11075-008-9196-5|bibcode=2008NuAlg..49..159G |s2cid=6314057 }}</ref>
